def: Fraction of all predictions that are correct: (TP + TN) / total. Misleading when classes are imbalanced.
Agreement between two groupings (e.g. clusters vs labels), ignoring the arbitrary cluster IDs. 1 = identical, ≈ 0 = chance, can be negative. **Not** an accuracy.
A controlled experiment comparing two alternatives on predefined criteria; participants are assigned to conditions and results compared.
Small count added to every feature count in Multinomial Naive Bayes so unseen words do not get probability 0: $(N_{cj}+\alpha)/(\sum N_{ck} + \alpha V)$. A hyperparameter.
A trivial reference model (e.g. always predict the most frequent class). A useful model must beat it.
The observations used to compute one parameter update.
$P(A\mid B) = P(B\mid A)P(A)/P(B)$. In classification: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior.
Each participant tests only one of the alternatives. Avoids learning effects across apps but needs more participants.
A sample drawn **with replacement** from the training rows; each tree of a random forest is trained on one.
Predicting a category (spam/not spam, species, digit).
Agreement between two annotators corrected for chance: $\kappa = (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e)$.
A variable that influences the outcome and is associated with the factor whose effect we study (e.g. prior experience with one tool).
Table of counts: rows = true class, columns = predicted class (scikit-learn). Diagonal = correct; off-diagonal = errors.
An isolated environment packaging an application with the software it needs; shares the host OS kernel. *VMs reproduce a machine; containers package an application environment.*
Letting half the participants use A first and half B first, so order/learning effects are spread over both conditions.
Classification loss: −log(probability given to the true class). Binary form: $-[y\log p + (1-y)\log(1-p)]$.
Split the training data into k folds; fit on k−1, validate on the remaining one, k times. Mean = performance, std = stability. Happens inside the training set.
Information not available at prediction time influences training or validation (e.g. using the final grade to predict passing). Gives unrealistically good results.
pandas' table: labelled rows (index) and named columns of possibly different types. One column is a Series.
A classifier that learns a sequence of yes/no questions (feature ≤ threshold). `max_depth` limits the number of questions.
The slope of the loss with respect to a parameter. Negative → increase the parameter; positive → decrease it.
How characters are stored as bytes: ASCII, UTF-8 (modern default), Latin-1/ISO-8859-1/CP1252 (older European files).
One complete pass of the training algorithm over the whole training set.
The number in `[n]:` next to a notebook cell: it was the n-th execution in the current kernel session.
Harmonic mean of precision and recall: $2PR/(P+R)$. High only if both are high.
An actual positive predicted as negative — a miss.
An actual negative predicted as positive — a false alarm.
A property of an observation given to the model as input (e.g. living area).
Selecting, creating and transforming raw information into useful features (e.g. building age, area per room, unit conversions).
Iteratively update parameters against the slope of the loss: $w \leftarrow w - \eta \cdot dL/dw$.
A setting chosen before training (learning rate, max_depth, K, C, α, number of trees), often tuned on validation data.
Sum of squared distances of points to their assigned K-means centroid. Lower = tighter; always decreases with more clusters.
The constant term $b$ in $\hat y = wx + b$: the prediction when all features are 0.
Unsupervised clustering: choose K, then alternate *assign to nearest centroid* and *move centroid to the mean*.
Supervised classifier: store labelled examples; predict by majority vote of the K closest ones. No training loop.
The running Python process behind a notebook: executes code, keeps variables in memory, runs inside one Python environment.
Orchestrates many containers across machines: deploy, scale, connect, recover.
The correct answer for an observation in supervised learning.
Size of each gradient-descent step. Too small → slow; too large → overshoot or diverge.
How plausible the observed features are under a class: $P(x\mid c)$. Likelihoods need not sum to 1 across classes.
Predicts a number with $\hat y = w_1x_1 + \dots + w_nx_n + b$; usually trained by minimising MSE.
A **classifier**: linear score → sigmoid (or softmax) → probability → class. Trained by minimising log loss.
A number measuring how far predictions are from targets (MSE, log loss). Training minimises it.
Mean absolute error $\frac1n\sum|y-\hat y|$; same unit as the target.
$\frac1n\sum(\hat y - y)$: direction of errors (bias). >0 over-predicts, <0 under-predicts.
Mean squared error $\frac1n\sum(y-\hat y)^2$; penalises large errors; unit is squared.
Classifier: score = prior × product of per-feature likelihoods, assuming features are conditionally independent given the class. Fits by counting/averaging.
Approximates a document–term table as $W H$: documents as non-negative mixtures of topics, topics as weighted word patterns.
What training optimises (minimise MSE, maximise likelihood, …).
One case in the dataset (one apartment, one flower, one email).
Represent a categorical feature with one 0/1 column per category, avoiding a fake order.
The model learns noise of the training data: low training error, higher validation error.
A value learned from data during training (weights, intercept, split thresholds).
scikit-learn object chaining preprocessing and a model so preprocessing is fitted on training data only (prevents leakage).
Probability of a class after seeing the evidence: $P(c\mid x)$ = likelihood × prior, normalised.
Of everything predicted positive, the fraction that really is positive: TP/(TP+FP).
How common a class is before seeing the features; estimated from the training labels.
Many decision trees trained on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets; their class probabilities are averaged.
Of all actual positives, the fraction found: TP/(TP+FN).
Predicting a number (rent, fuel, demand).
Penalty on large weights (L2: λΣw²) to reduce overfitting. In scikit-learn's LogisticRegression, smaller C = stronger.
Others can recreate your results: describe environments (requirements, Dockerfile), fix seeds, and make notebooks pass Restart & Run All.
$\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})$: squashes a score into a probability between 0 and 1; σ(0) = 0.5.
How well a point fits its own cluster vs the nearest other one: +1 well separated, 0 in between, <0 maybe misassigned.
Turns one score per class into probabilities summing to 1: $e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}$.
A split that keeps the class proportions equal in training and test sets (`stratify=y`).
Learning from features **and** known targets (regression, classification).
10-statement questionnaire, 5-point Likert, score 0–100: (Σ(odd−1) + Σ(5−even)) × 2.5. ~68 is average; not a percentage.
The value the model should predict.
Data held out from training and model selection, used once to estimate performance on unseen data.
Term weight = frequency in this document × inverse document frequency: distinctive words get high weight, words in every document low.
Decision rule turning a probability into a class (positive if p ≥ t). Moving it trades precision against recall without retraining.
Model too simple to capture the pattern: both training and validation errors are high.
Learning structure from features without targets (clustering, topic models, word vectors).
Data used to choose models and tune hyperparameters during development (or use cross-validation).
A per-project Python installation with its own packages. Isolates only the Python layer.
A software computer with its own OS. Packer builds images; Vagrant creates and manages development VMs.
Each participant tests all alternatives; controls individual differences, but needs counterbalancing for learning effects.
Learns a vector per word so that words in similar contexts get similar vectors (semantic space). Compare with cosine similarity.
The folder where relative file paths start (`os.getcwd()`). Wrong working directory → FileNotFoundError.
